# Book III, Proposition 10

*A circle does not cut a circle at more points than two*

[Euclid's proof](#euclids-proof) · [In Lean](#in-lean) · [What it rests on](#what-it-rests-on) · [Mishnah](#mishnah)

> A circle does not cut a circle at more points than two.

**In Lean:** ✅ proved, as Euclid states it · Euclid's argument, with one step changed

<p align="center"><em>Suppose two circles (red, blue) met at B, G, F, H: the red is a dashed oval, since no second circle can. Each black straight line, halving a yellow one at right angles, would pass through both centres: both at P, which III.5 forbids.</em></p>

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/III/10.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition III.10, with Heath's letters. Like Heath's, this figure draws the impossible supposition: DEF meeting ABC at four points, B, G, F, H, and so drawn as an oval, since no second circle can." width="360"></p>

<p align="center"><em>Like Heath's, this figure draws the impossible supposition: DEF meeting ABC at four points, B, G, F, H, and so drawn as an oval, since no second circle can.</em></p>

For, if possible, let the circle ABC cut the circle DEF at more points than two, namely B, G, F, H;

let BH, BG be joined and bisected at the points K, L,

and from K, L let KC, LM be drawn at right angles to BH, BG and carried through to the points A, E.

Then, since in the circle ABC a straight line AC cuts a straight line BH into two equal parts and at right angles,

the centre of the circle ABC is on AC. [III. 1, Por.]

Again, since in the same circle ABC a straight line NO cuts a straight line BG into two equal parts and at right angles,

the centre of the circle ABC is on NO.

But it was also proved to be on AC, and the straight lines AC, NO meet at no point except at P;

therefore the point P is the centre of the circle ABC.

Similarly we can prove that P is also the centre of the circle DEF;

therefore the two circles ABC, DEF which cut one another have the same centre P: which is impossible. [III. 5]

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.

**How the Lean follows the text**

- **Carried together.** "therefore the point P is the centre of the circle ABC." The rule gives ABC its centre, which the Lean names P at once; that AC and NO meet only there is the step above, so this sentence needs no Lean of its own.
- **Argued another way.** "therefore the two circles ABC, DEF which cut one another…" The Lean ends by `circle_eq` (Diagram-segment 2), from the common centre P and the common point B, instead of III.5. This is the converse Heath gives under III.5 (vol. 2, p. 12), and applies also to circles that only meet.

/-- If the angle BKC is right, so is the angle BKX for any other point X of the straight
line KC, on either side of K. -/
theorem Prop10.right_on_line {B K C X : Point} {N : Line} (hK : OnLine K N) (hC : OnLine C N)
    (hX : OnLine X N) (hKC : K ≠ C) (hXK : X ≠ K) (hB : ¬ OnLine B N) (hBKC : ∠ B K C = ∟) :
    ∠ B K X = ∟ := by
  have hBK : B ≠ K := fun e => hB (e ▸ hK)
  by_cases hb : Between X K C
  · have h := adjacent_eq_of_right hC hX (between_symm hb) hB
      (by rw [angle_symm hKC.symm hBK]; exact hBKC)
    rw [← h, angle_symm hKC.symm hBK]; exact hBKC
  · rw [angle_onRay_right ⟨hKC, hXK, ⟨N, hK, hC, hX⟩, hb⟩ hBK]; exact hBKC

/-- The straight lines at right angles to BH at K and to BG at L have at most one
common point. Euclid takes for granted that they are two straight lines; as in III.9
(`Prop9.apart`), were they one, the triangle BKL would have two right angles. -/
theorem Prop10.meet_once {B G H K L C O P Q : Point} (hBHG : Triangle B H G)
    (hBKH : Between B K H) (hBLG : Between B L G)
    (hC : ¬ Collinear B H C) (hBKC : ∠ B K C = ∟) (hO : ¬ Collinear B G O)
    (hBLO : ∠ B L O = ∟)
    (hKCP : Collinear K C P) (hKCQ : Collinear K C Q) (hLOP : Collinear L O P)
    (hLOQ : Collinear L O Q) : P = Q := by
  refine Classical.byContradiction fun hPQ => ?_
  obtain ⟨M₁, hK₁, hC₁, hP₁⟩ := hKCP
  obtain ⟨M₂, hK₂, hC₂, hQ₂⟩ := hKCQ
  obtain ⟨M₃, hL₃, hO₃, hP₃⟩ := hLOP
  obtain ⟨M₄, hL₄, hO₄, hQ₄⟩ := hLOQ
  obtain ⟨BH, hB_BH, hH_BH⟩ := Postulate1 B H (ne_of_between_ends hBKH)
  have hK_BH := on_line_of_between_ends hBKH hB_BH hH_BH
  obtain ⟨BG, hB_BG, hG_BG⟩ := Postulate1 B G (ne_of_between_ends hBLG)
  have hL_BG := on_line_of_between_ends hBLG hB_BG hG_BG
  have hKC : K ≠ C := fun e => hC ⟨BH, hB_BH, hH_BH, e ▸ hK_BH⟩
  have hLO : L ≠ O := fun e => hO ⟨BG, hB_BG, hG_BG, e ▸ hL_BG⟩
  obtain rfl := line_unique hKC hK₁ hC₁ hK₂ hC₂
  obtain rfl := line_unique hLO hL₃ hO₃ hL₄ hO₄
  obtain rfl := line_unique hPQ hP₁ hQ₂ hP₃ hQ₄
  /- Now one straight line, `M₁`, passes through K, C, L and O. -/
  have hKL : K ≠ L := by
    rintro rfl
    have hBK : B ≠ K := ne_of_between hBKH
    exact hBHG ⟨BH, hB_BH, hH_BH, (line_unique hBK hB_BG hL_BG hB_BH hK_BH) ▸ hG_BG⟩
  have hB : ¬ OnLine B M₁ := fun hB =>
    hC ⟨BH, hB_BH, hH_BH,
      (line_unique (ne_of_between hBKH) hB hK₁ hB_BH hK_BH) ▸ hC₁⟩
  have h₁ : ∠ B K L = ∟ := Prop10.right_on_line hK₁ hC₁ hL₃ hKC hKL.symm hB hBKC
  have h₂ : ∠ B L K = ∟ := Prop10.right_on_line hL₃ hO₃ hK₁ hLO hKL hB hBLO
  have h17 := (BookI.Prop17 (Triangle.of_line hK₁ hL₃ hKL hB).cab).1
  rw [h₁, angle_symm hKL (fun e => hB (by rw [e]; exact hL₃)), h₂] at h17
  exact lt_irrefl _ h17

```lean
/-- A circle does not cut a circle at more points than two. -/
theorem Prop10 {B G H : Point} {ABC DEF : Circle}
    (hB₁ : OnCircle B ABC) (hB₂ : OnCircle B DEF)
    (hG₁ : OnCircle G ABC) (hG₂ : OnCircle G DEF) (hH₁ : OnCircle H ABC)
    (hH₂ : OnCircle H DEF) (hBG : B ≠ G) (hBH : B ≠ H) (hGH : G ≠ H) :
    ABC = DEF := by
  -- For, if possible, let the circle ABC cut the circle DEF at more points than two, namely B,
  -- G, F, H;
  refine Classical.byContradiction fun hne => ?_
  /- Three common points suffice; Euclid never uses the fourth, F. -/
  have hBHG : Triangle B H G := Prop2.triangle hB₁ hH₁ hG₁ hBH hGH.symm hBG
  -- let BH, BG be joined and bisected at the points K, L,
  obtain ⟨BH, hB_BH, hH_BH⟩ := Postulate1 B H hBH
  obtain ⟨BG, hB_BG, hG_BG⟩ := Postulate1 B G hBG
  obtain ⟨K, hBKH, hBK⟩ := BookI.Prop10 hBH
  obtain ⟨L, hBLG, hBL⟩ := BookI.Prop10 hBG
  have hK_BH := on_line_of_between_ends hBKH hB_BH hH_BH
  have hL_BG := on_line_of_between_ends hBLG hB_BG hG_BG
  -- and from K, L let KC, LM be drawn at right angles to BH, BG and carried through to the
  -- points A, E.
  obtain ⟨X, hXG, hKX⟩ := BookI.Prop11 hBH ⟨BH, hB_BH, hH_BH, hK_BH⟩ hBHG
  obtain ⟨Y, hYH, hLY⟩ := BookI.Prop11 hBG ⟨BG, hB_BG, hG_BG, hL_BG⟩ hBHG.acb
  have hX_BH : ¬ OnLine X BH := hXG.triangle.off_line hB_BH hH_BH
  have hY_BG : ¬ OnLine Y BG := hYH.triangle.off_line hB_BG hG_BG
  have hKX_ne : K ≠ X := fun e => hX_BH (e ▸ hK_BH)
  have hLY_ne : L ≠ Y := fun e => hY_BG (e ▸ hL_BG)
  have hK_in : InsideCircle K ABC := Prop2 hB₁ hH₁ K hBKH
  have hL_in : InsideCircle L ABC := Prop2 hB₁ hG₁ L hBLG
  obtain ⟨AC, hK_AC, hX_AC⟩ := Postulate1 K X hKX_ne
  obtain ⟨A, hA, hA_AC, hAKX⟩ := line_circle_beyond hK_in hK_AC hX_AC hKX_ne.symm
  obtain ⟨C, hC, hC_AC, hCKA⟩ := line_circle_beyond hK_in hK_AC hA_AC (ne_of_between hAKX)
  obtain ⟨NO, hL_NO, hY_NO⟩ := Postulate1 L Y hLY_ne
  /- N is on H's side of BG, and O on the other side, as in the figure. -/
  obtain ⟨O, hO, hO_NO, hOLY⟩ := line_circle_beyond hL_in hL_NO hY_NO hLY_ne.symm
  obtain ⟨N, hN, hN_NO, hNLO⟩ := line_circle_beyond hL_in hL_NO hO_NO (ne_of_between hOLY)
  have hBK_ne : B ≠ K := ne_of_between hBKH
  have hBL_ne : B ≠ L := ne_of_between hBLG
  have hBKC : ∠ B K C = ∟ := by
    rw [angle_onRay_right (OnRay.of_between_between hAKX (between_symm hCKA)) hBK_ne]
    exact hKX B ⟨BH, hB_BH, hH_BH, hB_BH⟩ hBK_ne
  have hB_NO : ¬ OnLine B NO := fun h =>
    hY_BG ((line_unique hBL_ne h hL_NO hB_BG hL_BG) ▸ hY_NO)
  have hYLB : ∠ Y L B = ∟ := by
    rw [angle_symm hLY_ne.symm hBL_ne]
    exact hLY B ⟨BG, hB_BG, hG_BG, hB_BG⟩ hBL_ne
  have hBLO : ∠ B L O = ∟ :=
    (adjacent_eq_of_right hY_NO hO_NO (between_symm hOLY) hB_NO hYLB).symm.trans hYLB
  have hKC : K ≠ C := (ne_of_between hCKA).symm
  have hLO : L ≠ O := (ne_of_between hOLY).symm
  have hC_off : ¬ Collinear B H C := fun ⟨M, h1, h2, h3⟩ => hX_BH (by
    have e₁ := line_unique hBH h1 h2 hB_BH hH_BH
    have hK_M : OnLine K M := e₁ ▸ hK_BH
    have e₂ := line_unique hKC hK_M h3 hK_AC hC_AC
    exact e₁ ▸ e₂ ▸ hX_AC)
  have hO_off : ¬ Collinear B G O := fun ⟨M, h1, h2, h3⟩ => hY_BG (by
    have e₁ := line_unique hBG h1 h2 hB_BG hG_BG
    have hL_M : OnLine L M := e₁ ▸ hL_BG
    have e₂ := line_unique hLO hL_M h3 hL_NO hO_NO
    exact e₁ ▸ e₂ ▸ hY_NO)
  -- Then, since in the circle ABC a straight line AC cuts a straight line BH into two equal
  -- parts and at right angles,
  -- the centre of the circle ABC is on AC. [III. 1, Por.]
  obtain ⟨P, hP⟩ := exists_centre ABC
  have hP_AC : Collinear K C P := Prop1.porism hP hB₁ hH₁ hBKH hBK hC_off hBKC
  -- Again, since in the same circle ABC a straight line NO cuts a straight line BG into two
  -- equal parts and at right angles,
  -- the centre of the circle ABC is on NO.
  have hP_NO : Collinear L O P := Prop1.porism hP hB₁ hG₁ hBLG hBL hO_off hBLO
  -- But it was also proved to be on AC, and the straight lines AC, NO meet at no point except
  -- at P;
  /- AC and NO are two straight lines (`Prop10.meet_once`), so any point on both is P,
     even if P is K or L. -/
  have hmeet : ∀ Q : Point, Collinear K C Q → Collinear L O Q → Q = P :=
    fun Q hQ_AC hQ_NO =>
      Prop10.meet_once hBHG hBKH hBLG hC_off hBKC hO_off hBLO hQ_AC hP_AC hQ_NO hP_NO
  -- therefore the point P is the centre of the circle ABC.
  /- The centre the rule gives the circle ABC has already been named P. -/
  -- Similarly we can prove that P is also the centre of the circle DEF;
  obtain ⟨P', hP'⟩ := exists_centre DEF
  have hP'_AC : Collinear K C P' := Prop1.porism hP' hB₂ hH₂ hBKH hBK hC_off hBKC
  have hP'_NO : Collinear L O P' := Prop1.porism hP' hB₂ hG₂ hBLG hBL hO_off hBLO
  obtain rfl : P' = P := hmeet P' hP'_AC hP'_NO
  -- therefore the two circles ABC, DEF which cut one another have the same centre P: which is
  -- impossible. [III. 5]
  /- The common centre P and common point B identify the circles by `circle_eq`.
     The restated III.5 requires crossing, while this statement allows circles that only meet. -/
  exact hne (circle_eq hP hP' hB₁ hB₂ rfl)
  -- Therefore etc.
  -- Q. E. D.
```

**Reading the figure**

- [`between_cases`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L74) (through [`Prop2.triangle`](../../Elements/BookIII/Prop02.lean#L136)): Of three different points on a straight line, one is between the other two. (Between 6)
- [`between_of_between_left`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L66): If B is between A and C, and D is between A and B, then D is between A and C. (Between 4)
- [`between_of_between_right`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L70): If B is between A and C, and C is between B and D, then B is between A and D. (Between 5)
- [`between_of_inside_chord`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L155): A straight line through a point inside a circle has that point between the points where it meets the circle. (Circle 1)
- [`between_symm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L43) (used here): If B is between A and C, it is between C and A. (Between 1)
- [`centre_inside`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L35): The centre of a circle is inside it. (Generalities 3)
- [`circles_meet`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L201): If each circle passes through a point inside the other, the circles cut one another. This is the step Euclid takes for granted in I.1. (Intersection 5)
- [`circles_meet_same_side`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L97): Two circles that cut one another do so on each side of the straight line through their centres. (Intersections 8)
- [`exists_centre`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L75) (used here): Every circle has a centre. A rule of our own, not one of System E's: its content is Euclid's Definitions I.15 and I.16.
- [`exists_point`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L28): Let a point be taken. (Points 1)
- [`exists_point_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L40): Let a point be taken between B and C. (Points 3)
- [`exists_point_opposite_side`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L48): Let a point be taken on the other side of L from B. (Points 6)
- [`exists_point_same_side`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L44): Let a point be taken on the same side of L as B. (Points 5)
- [`inside_not_on`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L38) (through [`Prop2.triangle`](../../Elements/BookIII/Prop02.lean#L136)): A point inside a circle is not on it. (Generalities 4)
- [`line_circle_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L85): A straight line through a point B inside a circle, heading out to a point C outside it, cuts the circle between B and C. (Intersections 4)
- [`line_circle_beyond`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L91) (used here): A straight line through a point B inside a circle, produced beyond B away from C, cuts the circle there. (Intersections 5)
- [`line_unique`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L28) (used here): Two points determine a straight line. (Generalities 1)
- [`lines_meet_of_opposite_sides`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L179): A straight line joining points on opposite sides of L crosses L. (Intersection 1)
- [`ne_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L46) (used here): A point between two others differs from the first. (Between 1)
- [`ne_of_between_ends`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L49) (used here): The ends of a finite straight line differ. (Between 1)
- [`not_between_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L52): If B is between A and C, then A is not between B and C. (Between 1)
- [`not_between_of_between_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L79) (through [`OnRay.of_between_between`](../../Elements/Figure/Rays.lean#L86)): If B is between A and C, and also between A and D, then B is not between C and D: C and D lie on the same side of B. (Between 7)
- [`not_on_line_of_same_side`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L92) (through [`SameSideOf.triangle`](../../Elements/Figure/Sides.lean#L59)): Points on one side of a straight line are not on it. (Same side 3)

- [`on_line_of_between_ends`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L61) (used here): A straight line through A and C passes through every point between them. (Between 3)
- [`pasch2`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L111): If B is between A and C, A is on L and B is off it, then B and C are on the same side of L: a straight line that leaves L at A does not cross it again. (Pasch 2)
- [`pasch3`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L114): A straight line through a point between A and C separates them. (Pasch 3)
- [`pasch4`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L119): If two different straight lines L and M meet at B, and A and C are points of M, different from each other and from B, that are not on the same side of L, then B is between A and C. (Pasch 4)

- [`same_side_refl`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L85): A point off a straight line is on the same side of it as itself. (Same side 1)
- [`same_side_symm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L89): If A is on the same side of a straight line as B, then B is on the same side as A. (Same side 2)
- [`same_side_trans`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L96): Two points on the same side of a straight line as a third point are on the same side as each other. (Same side 4)
- [`triple_incidence1`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L131): Take B on L, C on M and D on N, three straight lines through A. If C lies within the angle BAD (on D's side of L and on B's side of N), then B and D are not on the same side of M: the straight line AC separates them. (Triple incidence 1)
- [`triple_incidence2`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L139): Take B on L, C on M and D on N, three straight lines through A, with B other than A and D off M. If C and D are on the same side of L, and B and D are not on the same side of M, then B and C are on the same side of N: C lies within the angle BAD. (Triple incidence 2)

**Lengths, angles and areas**

- [`adjacent_eq_of_right`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L67) (used here): A right angle is equal to the angle adjacent to it. (Diagram-angle 3; the other half is Definition 10 together with Postulate 4)
- [`angle_add_of_inside`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L54): If D lies within the angle BAC, then BAC is made up of BAD and DAC. (Diagram-angle 2)
- [`angle_eq_of_same_rays`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L72) (through [`angle_onRay_right`](../../Elements/Figure/Angles.lean#L47)): The angle doesn't change if its arms are traced through other points on the same rays. (Diagram-angle 4)
- [`angle_symm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L26) (used here): The angle ABC is the angle CBA. (Metric 4)
- [`area_congruent`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L43): Triangles equal in all their sides and angles are equal in area. Euclid uses this without comment once he has shown two triangles congruent. (Metric 9)
- [`area_rotate`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L35): The triangle ABC is the triangle CAB. (Metric 8)
- [`area_swap`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L38): The triangle ABC is the triangle ACB. (Metric 8)
- [`circle_eq`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L24) (used here): A circle is fixed by its centre and its radius. (Diagram-segment 2)
- [`eq_of_len_eq_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L17): A finite straight line with distinct ends has length. (Metric 1)
- [`inside_of_len_lt`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L33): A point nearer the centre than the circumference is inside. (Diagram-segment 4)
- [`len_add_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L21): If B is between A and C, then AB and BC together make up AC. (Diagram-segment 1)
- [`len_lt_of_inside`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L37): A point inside is nearer the centre than the circumference. (Diagram-segment 4)
- [`len_self`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L20): The "straight line" from a point to itself has no length. (Metric 1)
- [`len_symm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L23): The straight line AB is the straight line BA. (Metric 3)
- [`same_ray_of_angle_eq_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L49): If the angle BAC is nothing, C lies on the ray from A through B. (Diagram-angle 1)

**Superposition**

- [`superposition`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Superposition.lean#L30): **Superposition.** The triangle ABC can be applied to the straight line L with A on D, B on the ray from D through G, and C on the side of L where H is, without changing any side or angle.

**Laws of magnitude**

- [`add_assoc`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L23): Adding three magnitudes in a row, it makes no difference whether the first two or the last two are added first. (System E §3.5)
- [`add_comm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L26): The order of adding does not matter. (System E §3.5)
- [`add_lt_add_right`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L45): Adding the same thing to both sides keeps "less than". (System E §3.5)
- [`add_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L29): Adding nothing changes nothing. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_irrefl`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L32) (used here): No magnitude is less than itself. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_trans`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L35): What is less than the less is less still. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_trichotomy`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L39): Of two magnitudes, one is less, or they are equal, or the other is less. (System E §3.5)
- [`not_lt_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L42): Nothing is less than zero. (System E §3.5)

</details>

## Mishnah

_Our commentary: what Euclid assumes, what Lean made us say out loud, and how the result looks by modern means._

**Three points suffice.** Euclid supposes two circles meeting at four points, B, G, F and H, and uses three. He joins BH and BG, bisects them at K and L, and draws KC and LM at right angles to them. By the porism to III.1 the centre of each circle lies on both straight lines. They meet only at P, so both circles have that centre, which Euclid rules out by III.5. F never enters the argument. We state the conclusion positively: two circles with three distinct common points are one circle. Our figure keeps Heath's oval for DEF, since no second circle can meet ABC in the four points the supposition asks for.

Heath observes that the demonstration needs only meeting, whether the circles cut or touch (vol. 2, p. 23). Our statement keeps that scope. This matters at the last step: our III.5 asks that the circles cross, with a point of each within the other, while III.10 is given only common points. Once both centres are P, the Lean uses `circle_eq` directly. One centre and the common point B make the radii equal and hence make the circles one. This is the converse Heath gives under III.5 (vol. 2, p. 12), and a change to Euclid's final inference. The construction and the argument locating the centres remain his.

**Why do the perpendiculars meet?** Heath points out that Euclid assumes their meeting at P without proof (vol. 2, p. 24). The rule `exists_centre` gives each circle a centre, and the porism puts each centre on both perpendiculars, supplying a meeting point. We must still show that AC and NO are different straight lines. Were they one, the triangle BKL would have two right angles, contrary to I.17 (`Prop10.meet_once`). Their unique meeting then identifies the two centres.

**The modern way.** Subtract the equations of two different circles. If their centres differ, their common points lie on a straight line, the radical axis, which meets either circle at at most two points. If their centres agree, their radii differ and they have no common point. Three distinct common points therefore force the circles to coincide.

## Further reading

- For the radical axis of the modern way, found just as there by subtracting one circle's equation from the other's, and at right angles to the line of centres, S. L. Loney's [*The Elements of Coordinate Geometry*](https://archive.org/details/elementsofcoordi00lone) (1895, free online), ch. IX, "Systems of Circles", Art. 183 (p. 161), a clear Victorian textbook that does with equations what Book III does with figures.
- For the radical axis as the line where a point's powers with respect to two circles agree, I. M. Yaglom's [*Geometric Transformations IV: Circular Transformations*](https://doi.org/10.5948/UPO9780883859582) (2009), ch. 3, "Pencils of circles. The radical axis of two circles" (pp. 49–51), which introduces reflection in a circle by analogy with reflection in a line.
